episodes.210763: A line of thunderstorms tracked east through Middle Tennessee during the afternoon of April 4, 2026. These thunderstorms were initially weak as they tracked through west Middle Tennessee, but they strengthened once east of Nashville. The strongest portion of the line was located in Wilson and Macon counties where several reports of downed trees, utility lines, and minor roofing damage was received.
episodes.211275: A southward moving cold front and retreating dryline combined to create thunderstorms late on the evening of the third. A quasi-line of storms developed initially across the extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle and moved east-southeast. Strong instability allowed some of these scattered thunderstorms to become severe producing hail up to the size of half dollars and wind gusts up to 65 mph.
episodes.211373: Heavy rain fell across parts of northern Illinois during the evening of April 3rd into the early morning of April 4th, which caused localized flooding. The heaviest rains fell along the Interstate 55 corridor where an axis of 2 to 3 inches of rainfall occurred.
episodes.211678: An isolated severe storm developed on Saturday on the fourth of April.
episodes.211763: A high-amplitude (closed) upper storm system moved eastward across the Rockies on the 3rd and fostered a severe convective episode across portions of Oklahoma and western-north Texas. Initial thunderstorm development during the afternoon focused along a cold front from southwest into north-central Oklahoma, with a mix of multicell and supercell storm modes producing hail. Later in the evening, an intense complex of thunderstorms moved from west-central into east-central Oklahoma, including across the Oklahoma City Metropolitan area. This cluster produced swaths of damaging winds and several tornadoes. By the late evening, increasing frontal thunderstorms moved towards the Red River, producing intermittent wind gusts/damage and flooding.
episodes.211764: A high-amplitude (closed) upper storm system moved eastward across the Rockies on the 3rd and fostered a severe convective episode across portions of Oklahoma and western-north Texas. Initial thunderstorm development during the afternoon focused along a cold front from southwest into north-central Oklahoma, with a mix of multicell and supercell storm modes producing hail. By the late evening, increasing frontal thunderstorms moved towards the Red River, producing intermittent wind gusts/damage and flooding.
episodes.211797: Minor wind damage occurred in a few areas along the Red River associated with thunderstorms which accompanied a cold front.
episodes.211934: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 3rd, as a cold front moved into the area. These thunderstorms organized into a squall line as they moved east into eastern Oklahoma during the late evening of the 3rd and early morning hours of the 4th. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind in Sequoyah County.
episodes.211935: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed over central Oklahoma during the afternoon of the 3rd, as a cold front moved into the area. These thunderstorms organized into a squall line as they moved through eastern Oklahoma during the late evening of the 3rd and into northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 4th. The strongest thunderstorms produced damaging wind in Crawford and Sebastian Counties.
episodes.212145: Showers and isolated thunderstorms exiting central Indiana encountered a air mass characterized by low instability but high shear. This was enough to produce a tornado that moved through downtown Defiance.
episodes.212146: Rounds of rain and thunderstorms on the 4th resulted in at least two instances of flooding. At Benton Harbor, 1.90 inches of rain was recorded on the 4th, preceded by about 1 inch of rain from March 31 through April 3.
episodes.212202: A cold front moved across Southeast Michigan during the late afternoon and early evening of April 4. This triggered two lines of thunderstorms that caused pockets of damage south of I-94. The most significant storm occurred in Wayne County, producing an EF-1 tornado in Van Buren Township. The system also dumped 1 to 3 inches of rain, with some areas seeing up to 4 inches. Because the region had already received 3 to 5 inches over the previous five days, these additional downpours caused the Tittabawassee, Clinton, and Flint rivers to overflow. In addition, significant localized flooding occurred on already saturated ground, with the hardest-hit area being northwest Oakland County, specifically in and around Holly.
episodes.212220: A cluster of thunderstorms produced strong and gusty winds in far northwest Alabama during the early to mid afternoon hours.
episodes.212326: An isolated severe storm over Dale county resulted in a few trees down blocking roadways.
episodes.212328: A thunderstorm moving through the Detroit River produced a wind gust near 40 knots.
episodes.212450: At the surface, a low wobbled eastward from southern QC to northern ME. This allowed the trailing cold front to sweep generally southeastward across northern OH and northwest PA toward southern OH and southwestern PA. Along and ahead of the front, clusters of multicell thunderstorms persisted generally eastward across interior northern OH and generated isolated straight-line convective wind damage and marginally-severe hail in Marion, Morrow, and Holmes Counties. These thunderstorms occurred in a relatively-warm and moist sector comprised of weak to moderate MUCAPE and moderate effective bulk shear.
episodes.212777: A wet pattern developed during the first days of the month as above normal moisture, a nearby upper-level trough and a weak  trade wind cap supported shower and thunderstorm development. This included frequent passing showers across windward sectors, followed by enhanced afternoon convection. Flooding and Landslide reports where received during this period, April 1st to 5th.
episodes.212812: In the afternoon hours of April 4 and 5, reports indicated the presence of waterspouts across the local waters to the north and southeast of Puerto Rico.
episodes.212831: Despite considerable cloud cover across East Texas ahead of a cold front, relatively modest surface heating was ongoing by late morning on April 4th. A very moist air mass characterized by dew points in the upper 60s to lower 70s preceded the front. This environment supported scattered thunderstorm development along and ahead of the cold front, further aided by being on the southern fringe of the stronger mid-level winds helping propel the front. Additionally, MLCAPE values increasing to 1500+ J/kg and 25-35 knots of effective shear supported marginally organized storms capable of wind damage, flash flooding, and isolated tornadoes. However, poor mid-level lapse rates and a linear mode limited hail potential. As a result, one severe thunderstorm with quasi-supercell structure produced a brief tornado near Lindale in Smith County while a separate cluster of thunderstorms led to isolated flash flooding in Longview in Gregg County.

A spotter, chaser and an Oklahoma Highway Patrol officer each reported seeing this tornado near Interstate 44 and Interstate 240 on the southwest side of Oklahoma City. This tornado likely developed on the airport grounds of Will Rogers International Airport, south or southeast of the terminal building and moved east southeast, although thunderstorm wind damage was also observed on the airport grounds. After passing over Portland Avenue and damaging a road sign on Interstate 44, the tornado then hit Oklahoma City Community College (OCCC) breaking a few windows on campus. Continuing east-southeast, the tornado damaged roofs and trees near SW 81st Street and Villa Avenue, and damaged a mobile home near SW 82nd Street and Pennsylvania Avenue.

Damage to trees and a few power lines was noted |as the tornado curved to the northeast. A tree was uprooted just south |of Garretts Lake Road and US Highway 177 north of Shawnee. The tornado |dissipated a short time later.

A few minutes after the tornado near Dale dissipated, a separate circulation was noted on radar, which tightened and moved to the south and southeast. This tornado likely began northwest of the Leo Avenue and Wolverine Road intersection. While moving to the southeast, sporadic EF0 damage to trees was noted on Leo Avenue, north of Garretts Lake Road. EF1 damage was assessed to a gas station awning along Oklahoma State Highway 18 and Westech Road.

The Village of Holly issued a local state of emergency after flooding damaged pumps at its Waste Water Treatment Plant and impacted hundreds of homes. Water levels rose high enough to enter backyards and sheds. In some neighborhoods, residents reported water reaching the floorboards of their homes. The Road Commission for Oakland County (RCOC) was forced to close North Holly Road (just north of Quick Road near Holly Middle School) on the evening of April 4. The closure remained in place for several days due to standing water and road instability.

A mini-supercell developed and produced a short-lived, small, but intense EF1 tornado east and northeast of Lindale, TX. The tornado began in a field just south of FM Road 16 West, downing some small tree limbs and snapping the trunk of a pecan tree. At this same location, significant roof damage, consisting of shingle and roof decking loss, occurred to a single-family residence, resulting in a rating of EF1. The tornado downed a few more tree limbs before crossing FM Road 16 West. A couple of homes in the Woodcrest subdivision sustained minor shingle damage. Home security cameras in this|subdivision recorded the tornado's passage. The tornado continued northeast and crossed Legion Hills Road. In this location, a second single-family home sustained significant roof damage corresponding to a rating of EF1. A large oak tree was also uprooted on this property. The tornado continued northeast sporadically downing large tree limbs. A few more tree limbs were downed before the tornado lifted near the intersection of FM Road 2710 and County Road 4107. The tornado had estimated maximum wind speeds of 97 mph, a path length of approximately 2.5 miles, and a path width of 32 yards.

A NWS damage assessment determined that an EF-1 rain-wrapped|tornado was embedded in a line of severe thunderstorms that went|through Defiance during the afternoon of April 4th. Beginning on|the southwest side of town, the tornado produced some minor|shingle/tree damage. At least one home was likely destroyed due|to a fallen tree. Sporadic, significant tree damage was observed|through Riverside Cemetery. The tornado then nearly paralleled S|Clinton St as it moved from southwest to northeast. The most|impressive damage was done near Davidson and S. Clinton St where|several trunks were snapped, a branch lodged into a roof, and|several wooden transmission lines were snapped. The circulation|continued into downtown Defiance, uprooting/snapping trees, and|producing minor to moderate roof damage to numerous businesses|including a large church, bank, and USPS building, among others.|Notable tree damage was done at the Old Fort before the tornado|crossed the river confluence. Video footage from residence|confirms a circulation made it across the river. Widespread|additional tree and roof damage was then noted in the|neighborhoods just north of the Maumee River and west of|Carpenter Rd. Finally, several trunks were snapped or uprooted in|the Eagle Rock Golf Course before the circulation appears to have|dissipated.

The tornado first touched down just south of Martz Road, between |Rawsonville Road and Hoeft Road. At its onset, it flipped a hayride trailer before continuing its northeast path toward Hull Road. The most concentrated EF-1 damage was found along and just south of Hull Road, specifically between Elwell Road and Bak Road. Maximum estimated winds of 100 mph. In this area, surveyors observed multiple uprooted and snapped hardwood and pine trees, several snapped telephone poles, and a large barn that sustained significant damage, including a wall being completely blown out. The tornado continued northeast, crossing Sumpter Road where it downed power lines and several large tree limbs. The circulation lifted shortly after, just before reaching Savage Road on the western edge of Belleville.
